study.title: Psalm 23 The Lord, Shepherd and faithful Host
study.overview: This psalm of confidence presents the Lord as a Shepherd who supplies, guides, protects and leads his people to lasting communion with him. The poem advances from images of daily care to a table scene prepared before enemies, and ends with the certainty that God's goodness will accompany the psalmist throughout life. The axis of the psalm is trust: even in danger, lack, wear and opposition, the presence of God is enough.

outline.title: The Shepherd who supplies and gives rest
outline.explanation: The psalmist claims that the Lord is his Shepherd and therefore will not lack the necessary. The image of green pastures and quiet waters communicates provision, rest and security for the life of the flock.

outline.title: The Shepherd who restores and guides in danger
outline.explanation: God restores the soul and leads by straight paths, not only for human benefit, but because of his name. Even in the valley of the shadow of death, God's presence overcomes fear and comforts with rod and staff.

outline.title: The host who honors, guards and remains
outline.explanation: The figure changes to that of a banquet: God prepares a table before the adversaries and honors his servant with oil and overflowing cup. The outcome is the confidence that goodness and mercy will accompany the psalmist and that he will dwell in the house of the LORD for a long time.

study.context: The title attributes the psalm to David, and the notes describe him as a psalm of trust and security in the Lord, much appreciated by the people of God. One of the notes also notes that some readers relate it to a scenario of national liberation or restoration, but this is presented as a possibility, not as a certainty of the text. The psalm itself uses two great images: that of the pastor and that of the host who offers a banquet.
study.theology: The psalm teaches that God not only gives good things; he himself is the guarantee of good. His provision is personal and continuous: it feeds, leads, restores and protects. The divine direction is not arbitrary: he guides the path of justice for love of his name, which connects God's care to his faithfulness and reputation. In the final verse, "goodness" and "mysore" are presented as active companions of the believer throughout life, showing that the grace of God is not occasional. Communion culminates in remaining in the house of the LORD, an image of belonging, security, and prolonged enjoyment of the divine presence. In evangelical Christian reading, the psalm also points to the Messianic care of God with his people, without denying first the poetic and devotional meaning of the psalm itself.

scholarViews.insight: Verse 6 shows that the LORD expresses his faithful love through the goodness of his presence and the benefits he can bestow, stronger than the temporary trials caused by enemies.

In verse 1, David takes God as his Shepherd and, from this relationship, learns to expect all that is really good; the commentary highlights that the believer should be encouraged in the Lord from this relationship and the experience of his goodness.
In verse 6, goodness and mercy are seen as constant accompaniment throughout life, and the permanence in the house of the LORD is understood as continuity of communion and lasting happiness.

questions: If the Lord is my Shepherd, what fears and anxieties reveal that I do not yet fully trust in his provision?
How does the image of God as a host, in verse 5, correct my vision of suffering and opposition?
How can I live today in a consistent way with the certainty that the goodness and mercy of God accompany me?
study.practice: Recognize in prayer three forms of God's provision in your week: support, direction and comfort. Then, instead of just asking for relief, respond with practical confidence: abandon a dominating concern, choose a path of justice and practice daily gratitude. It is also appropriate to remember that the presence of God, and not the immediate absence of conflicts, is the center of the believer's security.
study.uncertainty: The given text brings the numbered psalm as 1 to 6, although in some biblical editions it has another division of verses. The notes allow only careful and summarized reading; it is not possible to safely affirm external historical details, nor to solve all the poetic nuances of expressions such as the valley of the shadow of death, "home of the LORD," "for many and many days" beyond what the chapter itself and the notes support.
